items.text: In this lesson you talk about your job, your week and what you have to do. You meet a new colleague, and you read a job advert and part of a contract. Then you ask the right questions about a new job before you say yes.

In this lesson you talk about your work and your week. First, you listen to Amina. It is her first day in a new job. Her colleague Tomasz welcomes her. Amina asks: What's the job like? Tomasz says: It's busy, but it's never boring. Then she asks: What do I have to do? Listen to have to. We say it fast, like one word. The v in have sounds like f.

There are two grammar points in this lesson. One. For every day and every week, say: I work, she starts. We answer calls from customers all day. For now, or for this week only, use am, is or are and -ing. This week I'm working on a new project. Two. Have to means there is no choice. I have to start at eight. She has to wear a uniform. Don't have to means it is not necessary. You don't have to wear a suit. It is your choice. Need to is like have to. I need to finish this report today.

Next, you read a job advert and part of a contract. The advert is short. It says the hours, the pay and what you need for the job. Read one line carefully: No experience needed. That means you don't have to have experience. It is good news. You can apply! Then you describe a job in three parts. What do you do? What do you have to do? And what is it like?

In the task, a new colleague asks about your job. Tell her what you do, what you have to do and what the job is like. Then a manager offers you a new job. Before you accept, ask questions. Do I have to work at weekends? Is there any overtime? Is it full-time or part-time? Ask before you sign the contract, not after.
Last, you read a story or an article about work. Read it once for the main idea. Then read it again and answer the questions.

In this lesson you are a host, and a guest comes to your flat. You invite people, offer drinks and snacks, and explain how something works. You also check what people mean, and you write an invitation and two replies.

In this lesson you are the host. A guest comes to your home. First, you listen to Mei. Her new neighbour, Kwame, comes for a drink on Saturday. Mei says: Come in! Would you like a cold drink, or a coffee? Kwame says: It's warm today, isn't it? The short question at the end is a tag. Kwame is sure. He only wants Mei to agree. So his voice goes down on the tag. Listen for it. Then Mei explains how the front door of the building works.

There are two grammar points in this lesson. One. To offer a thing, say: Would you like a coffee? Would you like a biscuit? To invite someone, add to and a verb: Would you like to come for dinner? Two. Instructions start with a verb: Press the button. Twist the key. To say what not to do, use don't: Don't push the door. Pull it. Put the steps in order: first, then, after that, finally.

Next, you read a notice in an office kitchen. Its title is: How to make tea for a guest. It has six steps. Most steps say what to do. Some say what not to do: Don't fill the kettle to the top. Read it slowly. The order of the steps is important. Then you write an invitation, and two replies. One reply says yes, and one says no. A polite no often starts with unfortunately.

In the task, you are the host. A new colleague comes to your home for a coffee. Welcome him, and offer drinks. Then explain how your coffee machine works, step by step. At the end, check that he understood. Ask: Is that clear? Or ask him to say the steps back to you. Then invite him to something else.
Last, you read a story or an article about hosts and guests. Read it once for the main idea. Then read it again and answer the questions.

In this lesson you get things done. You renew a card, fill in a form and report a fault in your home. You also say what you have and haven't done, and you cancel an appointment.

In this lesson you get things done: cards, forms and repairs. First, you listen to Samir. He is at a counter in a city office. He wants to renew his driving licence. The assistant asks: Have you filled in the form? Samir says: Yes, I've already filled it in. Then she asks: Have you signed it yet? Samir says: Not yet. Sorry! Listen for the short v in I've. It is quiet, but it is important.

There are two grammar points in this lesson. One. To say something is done, use have or has and a past form. I've posted the letter. She's signed the form. Already means it is done, maybe sooner than you think. I've already printed it. Yet is for questions and for not. Have you signed it yet? No, not yet. Still means it is not done, and it is late. I still haven't received my card. With a past time, like yesterday, use the past: I posted it yesterday. Two. To say why, use so that. Write clearly, so that we can read it.

Next, you read a notice at a counter. It tells you what to do before you join the queue. Then you read a repair form. Read every instruction. Block capitals are big letters, like this: A, B, C. Tick one box means one box only. Then you fill in the form. You also write a message to cancel an appointment.

In the task, it is your day off, and you have three errands. First, you renew your library card at a counter. Then you phone the housing office about a fault in your flat. The heating doesn't work. Say what you have already tried. Then book a time for the repair. Say why with so that: The morning, please, so that I can go to work after.
Last, you read a story or an article about getting things done. Read it once for the main idea. Then read it again and answer the questions.

In this lesson you arrange a meeting at work. You suggest a time, say no politely and say what you think will happen. Then the plan changes, so you move the meeting.

In this lesson you make plans with other people. Then you change them. First, you listen to two colleagues, Mei and Carlos. They need an hour next week to plan a training day. Mei asks: Are you free on Monday morning? Carlos looks at his diary. He says: I'm afraid I can't. The words I'm afraid make a no polite. Then Mei suggests another time: How about Tuesday afternoon? When they agree, Carlos says the day, the time and the place again. That is a good way to check.

This lesson has three ways to talk about the future. One: a plan with a day or a time, and another person knows about it. Use am, is or are, and a verb with -ing. I'm meeting a customer at ten. Two: something you decided, but did not arrange. Use going to. I'm going to book a room. Three: a guess. You think it, but you don't know it. Use will. I think it'll be busy. With a guess, say how sure you are. Definitely means very sure. Probably means nearly sure. Perhaps means not sure.

Next, you read a message thread from a team at work. Four people try to find a time for one meeting. The first day does not suit everyone. One person is visiting another office, so they move the meeting. Read it once, and find the day they choose. Then read it again, slowly, for the times. Then you write a message to move a meeting. Say sorry, give the reason, and suggest two new times.

In the task, you arrange a meeting with two colleagues, Kwame and Lena. Everybody has a busy week. Ask: Are you free on Wednesday? Suggest a time: How about three o'clock? If you can't come, say so politely. When you all agree, say the plan back: Wednesday at three, in Room 2. Then something changes. Say sorry, give the reason, and find a new time.

Last, you read a story or an article about plans. Look at the title first, and predict what will happen. Make a guess with will. Then read it once for the main idea. Read it again to answer the questions.

In this lesson things go wrong on the way to work. You tell a colleague what happened, and what was going on at the time. Then you read an incident record, and you phone your manager about a problem.

In this lesson things go wrong, and you tell people what happened. First, you listen to Omar. He arrives at work very late, and his colleague Lena asks why. Omar says: You'll never guess what happened! This tells Lena that a surprising story is coming. Lena asks: What happened then? When the news is bad, she says: Oh no! Listen to the end of the past verbs. Crashed ends in a t sound. Realised ends in a d sound. Waited has one more part: wait-ed.

In a story, one thing is often going on already. Then something happens in the middle of it. For the thing that was going on, use was or were, and an -ing verb. I was waiting for the bus. For the thing that happened, use the past. The call came. Join them with when. I was waiting when the call came. Or start with while. While I was waiting, the call came. Some past forms do not end in -ed. Teach becomes taught. Spend becomes spent. Hide becomes hid. Learn them in pairs, out loud.

Next, you read two short documents from a workplace. An incident record is a form. It says what happened, when and where, and what the staff did. A witness statement is one person's own words about what they saw. Read both. What do they both say? What does only one of them say? Then you write about a morning that went wrong. Tell the events in order.

In the task, you have a problem on the way to work. You phone your manager. Say sorry first. Then say where you are, and what happened. Say what you were doing: I was sitting on the bus when it stopped. Say when you will probably arrive. Then, at work, you fill in the incident record.

In this lesson you shop for your office and for yourself. You compare two models, ask for a cheaper one and ask about delivery. Then you choose between two phone plans, and explain your choice.

In this lesson you compare things, choose one and ask for what you need. First, you listen to Priya. She manages a small office, and the fridge in the staff kitchen is broken. In a big shop, she looks at two fridges. She asks: Which model is better? The assistant compares the two fridges. Then Priya asks: Is there a cheaper one? The cheaper one is smaller, but it is good value. That means a good price for what you get. At the end, she asks: Do you deliver? A fridge is too big to carry home.

To compare two things, short words add -er: cheap, cheaper. Longer words take more: more useful, more expensive. For one thing in a group, say the cheapest, or the most useful. This is the most useful phone in the shop. You can also say not as big as. The 200 isn't as big as the 300. So the 300 is bigger. For amounts, ask: can you count it? Bottles and people: a few, and fewer. Milk, time and space: a little, and less. Say fewer people, but less milk.

Next, you read a leaflet from a store. It explains its delivery service, in five steps. Look for the words van and lorry. A lorry is much bigger than a van. Then you read a short text that compares two shops. One is in the town centre. The other one is only online. Read carefully for the numbers: prices, days and the maximum. Then you write about something you bought. Say which shop you chose, and why.

In the task, your phone contract ends, and you choose between two new plans. Ask about the difference. Then compare them: Plan B has more data, but it's more expensive. Think about you. Do you use a little data, or a lot? How much can you pay each month? Then choose one plan, and give two reasons. For example: It's cheaper, and the contract isn't as long.

In this lesson you talk about your home, your neighbours and your health. You say how long something has been true: I've lived here for six years. You read a notice in a building, and you talk to a doctor.

In this lesson you talk about time. Not when something happened, but how long. First, you listen to two neighbours. Tomasz is new in the block. He moved in on Saturday. Amina lives on the ground floor. Tomasz asks her: How long have you lived here? Amina says: For six years. I've owned it since last summer. Listen to for and since. In a sentence, for is short and quick. Since is clear.

Amina came six years ago, and she still lives there. It started in the past, and it is still true now. For this, use have or has and the past form. I have lived. She has worked. He has had. Then use for or since. For goes with a length of time: for six years, for a week. Since goes with the start: since 2019, since Monday. To ask, say: How long have you lived here? Do not say: I live here since 2019. Say: I've lived here since 2019. You also learn somebody, nobody and everywhere. After everybody, the verb has an s: Everybody knows him.

Next, you read a notice in the hall of a block of flats. The lift has not worked since Monday. Then you read a short text: Getting better takes time. It explains an illness, an injury and treatment. Then you write about your home. How long have you lived there? What is the area like?

In the task, you are at the doctor's. You have a painful knee. The doctor asks: How long have you had it? You say: For three weeks. The doctor asks: What have you tried? You say: I've rested it, and I've taken some tablets. Then ask one question. Is it serious? How long will it take to get better?
Last, you read a story about home and health. Read it once for the story. Then read it again and answer the questions.

In this lesson you talk about how things were and how they made you feel. You learn the difference between boring and bored. You read a notice board and two references, and you write a short review.

In this lesson you talk about feelings. First, you listen to two colleagues, Priya and Kwame. It is Monday morning at work. Priya went on a photography course. Kwame asks: What was it like? Priya says: It was amazing. She was nervous at first, but everybody was friendly. Then Kwame talks about a film. He says: It was so boring! Listen to the long words. Each one has one strong part. Say that part louder.

Some words have two forms. The film was boring. I was bored. The -ing word tells you about the thing. The -ed word tells you how a person feels. So do not say: I was boring. That means other people were bored with you! Some words always have a small word after them. Good at. Interested in. Afraid of. Then you say how much. Quite good means good, but not very good. Too long means it was a problem. Not big enough means it was too small.

Next, you read a notice board at a library. It shows free sessions, and what people said about them. Then you read two references for the same man, Omar. One reference is long and warm. The other is very short. Which one helps Omar more? Look for the words about him: honest, reliable, calm and hard-working. Then you write a short review of a film, a course or a place.

In the task, a colleague wants to do something nice at the weekend. Tell her about a film, a course or a day out. What was it like? How did you feel? Say one good thing and one problem. Say how much, too. It was quite busy. The café was too crowded. Then say if you recommend it. Yes, it's worth it. Or: No, I wouldn't recommend it.
Last, you read a story about feelings. Read it once for the story. Then read it again and answer the questions.

In this lesson you give your opinion, and you agree and disagree politely. You ask for things at a desk with could and would. Then you write a polite note.

In this lesson you give your opinion, and you ask for things politely. First, you listen to two colleagues, Ana and Samir. The number 12 bus is going to change its route. Samir says: I think it's a good idea. Ana says: Sorry, I disagree. Later, Ana says: I agree, because I'm often late too. They both give a reason. That is the important part. Listen to their voices. When you are sure, your voice goes down at the end.

After I think, I hope and I'm sure, say a whole sentence. I think the bus is too slow. I hope they listen to us. For no, say: I don't think it's fair. To ask politely, use could or would. Could you help me? Would you mind waiting? Could is more polite than can. Mustn't and don't need to are different. You mustn't park here. It is not allowed. You don't need to pay. It is free, so it is not necessary.

Next, you read a short text: How to ask for something at a desk. It gives four steps. Start with Excuse me. Use could or would. Say thank you. And be patient. It also explains a difficult answer. Do you mind waiting? No, not at all. That means: yes, I can wait. Then you write a polite note. You ask for two things.

In the task, you visit another office. At reception, you ask for a visitor's pass and the Wi-Fi password. Use could, or would you mind, and say thank you. Then you are in a short meeting. Your manager asks: Should we start work at eight? Give your opinion and a reason. Then agree or disagree with a colleague. Say: I see your point, but I think …
Last, you read a story about asking and opinions. Read it once for the story. Then read it again and answer the questions.
Your bus company wants to change your bus route. What do you do?

I think it's a good idea.
Sorry, I disagree.
That's a good point.

I'm not sure.

In this lesson you learn how machines work, and the safety rules at work. You listen to a new worker and his supervisor. Then you read a notice and four signs, and show a new colleague a machine.

In this lesson you learn how things work, and the rules at work. First, you listen to Carlos. It is his first morning at a delivery company. His supervisor, Mei, gives him a scanner. Carlos asks: How does it work? Mei says: First, you press this button. Then she explains each step. Carlos asks: What happens if it doesn't beep? Listen for the answer. Mei also gives some rules. Listen for mustn't. In mustn't, you don't hear the first t.

There are two grammar points in this lesson. One: if, for things that happen every time. If you press this button, the screen comes on. Use the present in both parts. Do not use will after if. Two: rules. Must and have to mean: it is necessary. You must wear gloves. Mustn't and not allowed to mean: don't do it. You mustn't smoke here. Don't have to is different. It means: it is not necessary, but you can if you want.

Next, you read a notice on a machine in a staff kitchen. It says how to use the machine, and what can go wrong. Then you read four safety signs. Signs use very few words. No entry means: you mustn't go in. Then you write five steps for a machine you know. Start each step with a verb: press, put, wait. At the end, add one warning with if.

In the task, you are the expert. A new colleague starts work, and you show them a machine. Say the steps in order: first, then, after that. Say what happens if something goes wrong. Then give the safety rules, with must, mustn't and don't have to. At the end, check. Ask: Is that clear? Do you want to try?

In this lesson you plan a trip and book a seat and a room. You read a timetable, a platform notice and a weather warning. Then you deal with a cancelled train.

In this lesson you travel, and you deal with problems on the way. First, you listen to Priya. It is the evening before a work trip abroad. Her flight leaves tomorrow morning. She phones a coach company to book a seat to the airport. She asks: When does the first coach leave? It is too early, so she asks: Is there a later one? Listen carefully for the times. Fifteen and fifty sound different: fif-TEEN, FIF-ty.

In English, there are four ways to talk about the future. One: a time on a timetable. Use the present simple. The coach leaves at 6:10. Two: an arrangement, with a ticket or with a person. I'm flying to Lisbon tomorrow. Three: a plan from before. I'm going to pack tonight. Four: a decision you make as you speak, or a guess. I'll take the 6:10. You'll have time. Choose the right one, and people understand how fixed your plan is.

Next, you read three short documents from a station. The timetable says when the trains leave and arrive. Some run daily. One runs on Fridays and Saturdays only. Look at the days, not only the times. The platform notice says which trains are late or cancelled today. The weather warning says what the storm will do. Read it before you travel. Then you write a message about a delay. Say what happened, and give your new time.

In the task, you plan a trip for work. First, you read the timetable and choose a train. Then you book a ticket at the station, and a room at a hostel. But then there is a problem. Your train is cancelled. Ask the clerk: Is there a later one? Then call the hostel and give your new arrival time.
Last, you read a story or an article about a journey. Read it once for the story. Then read it again and answer the questions.

This is the last lesson of Level 2. It is about talking with people you don't know yet. First, you listen to Amina. She is new in her area, and she goes to a community group. A member, Kwame, starts a chat. He asks questions, and he really listens. When Amina tells a story, he says: Really? What happened next? When Amina doesn't understand, she asks: What do you mean? At the end, Kwame makes a suggestion: How about the cycling group? After How about, use a noun, or a verb with -ing. How about a walk? How about meeting on Sunday?

There are two grammar points in this lesson. One: Have you ever…? It asks about your whole life, up to now. Have you ever been to Scotland? Answer: Yes, I have. Or: No, I've never been there. Then ask for the details with the past simple. When did you go? What was it like? Two: verbs with a small word after them. Look after means take care of. Put off means move to later. Take up means start a new activity. With it, the small word goes last: put it off, take it up.

Next, you read a notice from the Riverside Community Group. It is for new members. It says what the group does, when the teams meet, and how to take part. Then you write a reply. Say who you are, and why you want to join. Then make one suggestion for a new activity or an event.

In the task, you go to your first meeting. A member comes to say hello. Introduce yourself, and keep the conversation going for three minutes. Ask questions, and react to the answers: Really? That's interesting! Ask one question with Have you ever…? At the end, suggest an activity.

Last, you read a story or an article about people who meet in a group. Read it once for the story. Then read it again and answer the questions. After this lesson comes the A2 review and check. Then you are ready for Level 3.
